title: Architecture Standards — Cross-cutting Guidelines and ADRs
author: Claire Mendoza
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards: API design, coding conventions, infrastructure (IaC) expectations, model-serving requirements, observability guidance, performance SLOs, and the Decision Record (ADR) process. It is intended for engineers, tech leads, and reviewers who design or operate services that serve LLM inference or supporting systems.

Scope

- Applies to all services and libraries owned by the inference, platform, and developer-experience teams.
- Includes hosted API endpoints, Dedicated/Private-serving control plane components, and first-line supporting infra (ingress, auth, telemetry, model registry).
- Does not replace language- or team-specific style guides; consider this a cross-cutting contract.

Principles

1. Predictability: APIs and infra must make performance and cost predictable.
2. Observability-first: ship metrics/traces/logs alongside feature code.
3. Fail-safe: degrade gracefully with clear fallbacks.
4. Reproducibility: infrastructure changes are IaC and fully reviewable.
5. Minimal blast radius: use isolation, quotas, and sensible defaults.

1) API Standards

Design and surface-level rules for public and internal REST/gRPC endpoints.

- URL and resource naming:
  - Use kebab-case for path segments: /v1/inference/jobs, /v1/models/{model-id}/versions.
  - Prefer nouns for resources; verbs belong to actions (e.g., POST /v1/inference -> create inference request).
- Versioning:
  - Major-version in path: /v1/. Breaking changes require a v2 path and an ADR (see ADR section).
  - Deprecation policy: announce 90 days before removing a minor-element; 180 days for breaking changes.
- Idempotency and request semantics:
  - POST that creates persisted work must accept Idempotency-Key header for safe retries.
  - Duplicate-detection window defaults to 10 minutes for inference job submission.
- Authentication and authorization:
  - All endpoints require bearer token via Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  - Use token scopes to gate sensitive operations (model upload, config change).
- Request/response patterns:
  - Use structured JSON with stable envelopes: {"data": <object>, "meta": {"request_id": "..."}}.
  - Avoid returning model-internal traces or KV cache contents.
- Error handling:
  - Use HTTP semantics: 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
  - Error response schema: {"error": {"code":"string", "message":"string", "details": []}}.
  - Provide machine-readable error codes for routing and automations.
- Rate limits and throttling:
  - Document per-route default rate limits in the route README.
  - On throttling, return Retry-After header with a human- and machine-friendly message.

2) Coding Standards

Language and style guidance intended to reduce review friction and ensure reliability.

- Supported languages and runtimes:
  - Primary server-side languages: Go (runtime components), Python (data/SDK work), TypeScript (console/SDK), Rust (performance-critical kernels).
- Linters and formatters:
  - Must pass configured linters in CI (golangci-lint, flake8/ruff, eslint, clippy).
  - Apply auto-formatting (gofmt, black, prettier) on pre-commit.
- Testing requirements:
  - Unit tests: target >80% statement coverage for new modules; critical libs should be higher.
  - Integration tests: all infra-facing changes require an integration test in CI.
  - E2E smoke: before merging major API changes run smoke harness against staging.
- Dependency policy:
  - Limit transitive dependencies; prefer well-maintained packages with security history.
  - Use Dependabot or similar for automated updates; major upgrades require security/compatibility review.
- Secrets and config:
  - Never check secrets into git. Use vault/KMS and environment variables injected at runtime.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, Networking, Secrets)

Conventions for Terraform, networking, and deployment patterns.

- IaC baseline:
  - All cloud infra must be provisioned via Terraform modules stored in eng-infra repo and reviewed through GitHub PRs.
  - Modules must include usage examples and variable descriptions.
- Environment separation:
  - Environments: dev, staging, prod. No direct prod changes outside PRs and approved pipelines.
- Networking and VPC:
  - Use explicit subnet tagging for inference clusters (eg: category=inference, tier=gpu).
  - Cross-region replication must follow the multi-region network design doc and use private endpoints.
- Secrets management:
  - Keys stored in HashiCorp Vault with short TTLs for dynamic credentials where possible.
- CI/CD:
  - Releases are built in CI with reproducible artifacts (image digest pinned).
  - Promote artifacts across environments; do not rebuild for each environment.

4) Model-serving Standards

Packaging, runtime expectations, and compatibility rules for models served by Redwood.

- Model artifacts and manifests:
  - Every model must include a manifest.json with schema_version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, input_signature. Example manifest entry: 
    {"schema_version":"1.0", "architecture":"transformer-llm", "quantization_profile":"int8-4g"}
- Model onboarding checklist:
  1. Validate model architecture and tokens with the onboarding harness.
  2. Run perf benchmark (latency & throughput) on target GPU class.
  3. Generate quantization profile and quality regression report vs baseline prompts.
  4. Create model entry in registry and ADR for unusual behavior.
- Quantization and profile guidance:
  - Preferred profiles: fp16 for high-quality workloads; int8 or int4 with quality guardrails for cost-sensitive paths.
  - Include representative eval prompt sets with each profile to allow automatic quality checks.
- Runtime constraints and resource labeling:
  - Models must declare expected peak context length; runtime will allocate kv-cache accordingly.
  - Tag models for fallback compatibility (e.g., compatible-with: [redwood-vx-small, redwood-vx-compat]).
- Fallback and graceful degradation:
  - If preferred model is unavailable, runtime should route to a compatible fallback model based on policy (latency-first vs cost-first).
  - All fallbacks must be audited and listed in the model registry entry.

5) Observability Standards

Telemetry and monitoring rules to ensure operability and efficient troubleshooting.

- Metrics (Prometheus-style):
  - Every service must expose: health_check (gauge), request_count (counter by route), request_latency_ms (histogram p50/p95/p99), error_count (counter by code).
  - Cardinality: keep label cardinality low (route, model_id, region). Avoid user_id or tenant_id as metric labels; use logs/traces instead.
- Tracing:
  - Distributed tracing required across service boundaries for inference flows. Propagate trace_id and request_id.
- Logs:
  - Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, msg, details.
  - PII must not be logged. Mask or redact inputs that include user data.
- Dashboards and alerts:
  - Standard dashboards: per-model latency, per-route QPS, error budget burn rate.
  - Alert guidelines (default thresholds):
    - High error rate: error_count > 5% of requests over 5m AND p95 latency > 2x baseline => P1 alert.
    - Resource saturation: GPU memory usage > 85% for > 5m => P1.
    - Slow degradation: p95 increase > 30% vs baseline for 15m => P2.
- On-call and runbook linkage:
  - Every alert should link to a runbook with triage steps and known mitigations.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Target SLOs for inference paths and guidance on how to measure and validate.

- Example SLO table:

  | Path | SLO (p95) | Error budget | Measurement window | Owner |
  |------|-----------|--------------|--------------------|-------|
  | Hosted text-generation (low-latency) | <= 150ms | 99.9% | 30d | inference-platform@redwood.com |
  | Chat (multi-turn) | <= 250ms | 99.5% | 30d | inference-platform@redwood.com |
  | Embeddings (bulk) | throughput: >= 2000 reqs/s per shard | 99.9% | 30d | embeddings-team@redwood.com |

- Batching and caching guidance:
  - Use request batching for high QPS endpoints; default batch window 10ms for low-latency routes with adaptive expand/contract logic.
  - Implement prefix/KV caching for repeated token prefixes; cache hit target >= 20% for conversational workloads where applicable.
- Benchmarking:
  - Benchmarks must include realistic token distributions (prompt lengths, response lengths) and warm/cold cache scenarios.
  - Report p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, and tokens/sec.

7) ADR Process and Examples

How to write, review, and store Architectural Decision Records. ADRs document important trade-offs and become part of the audit trail.

- ADR template (required fields):
  - title, status, context, decision, consequences, alternatives considered, date, authors, reviewers.
- Process:
  1. Draft ADR in the architecture repo under /adrs with the template.
  2. Add reviewers and link related docs (designs, benchmarks).
  3. Obtain at least two engineering reviewers and one product/security reviewer for infra-impacting decisions.
  4. Publish ADR to Confluence with links to code/PRs; include migration plan and owner.
- Example ADR summary (formatted as a table):

  | ADR ID | Title | Decision | Owner | Status | Date |
  |--------|-------|----------|-------|--------|------|
  | ADR-2026-03 | Model quantization default strategy | Adopt int8 runtime profile for non-critical hosted tiers with quality gating | Claire Mendoza | accepted | 2026-03-10 |

8) Review, Compliance and Exceptions

- Periodic review:
  - This document and related ADRs should be reviewed every 12 months or sooner after major infra changes.
- Exceptions:
  - Exceptions must be recorded in the exceptions registry and approved by platform engineering and security for infra/security-related deviations.

Appendix: Checklist for New Service or Model Onboarding

1. API: follows naming/versioning conventions, includes schema and example payloads.
2. Code: passes linters, unit/integration tests, and CI gates.
3. Infra: Terraform module created/updated, env separation confirmed.
4. Observability: metrics, traces, and logs instrumented; dashboards created.
5. Performance: benchmark report attached, meets SLO targets or has documented mitigation.
6. Security & data: secrets handled by Vault; PII redaction verified.
7. ADR: if the change is breaking or introduces systemic trade-offs, submit ADR and link to onboarding.
